**UMass Amherst — the architecture-search bill that was eighty-eight times too large (2019–2021)**

In 2019 Emma Strubell, Ananya Ganesh and Andrew McCallum of the University of Massachusetts Amherst published an ACL paper that put a price on training runs. One row did most of the damage. Neural architecture search: 274,120 hours on eight P100s, 626,155 lbs of CO2e, and an estimated cloud bill of $942,973 to $3,201,722. Beside it they set what the search had returned — the Evolved Transformer's state-of-the-art 29.7 BLEU on English-to-German translation, an increase of 0.1 BLEU over the model it displaced, for at least $150k of on-demand compute. Until then NAS papers had reported accuracy and treated the budget as an implementation detail.

The figure was an extrapolation, and that mattered. The authors had no measured energy draw for the search; they converted a reported search size into P100-GPU-hours and priced it at an average datacentre on an average grid.

In 2021 David Patterson and colleagues went back to the actual run. Measured, the Evolved Transformer search emitted 3.2 tCO2e rather than the 284 tCO2e implied — an overestimate of 88x. Two things explained it. The search never trained full-scale models: it evaluated candidates on small proxy tasks, so the per-trial cost assumed by the extrapolation was far too high. And it ran on TPU v2 inside a Google datacentre — hardware with roughly 5.6 to 6.2 times the performance per watt of a P100, in a facility with a PUE near 1.11 against an industry average around 1.59.

The correction demolished the headline and left the harder question standing. Even at 3.2 tCO2e the search consumed real capital, and the return on the flagship benchmark was a tenth of a BLEU point against a Transformer that had itself been tuned by hand. Nobody outside Google could have checked either number, because neither the search nor the paper reported a budget in a form anyone could audit. That is the point Patterson's team pressed: measure and publish, because extrapolation from an architecture description is unreliable in both directions.

When you run Optuna, ASHA or a DARTS supernet, this is the discipline the episode buys you. Report the search budget — trials, wall-clock, hardware, proxy-task fidelity — as a peer of the accuracy number rather than a footnote. Then answer the question your own table should provoke: how much of the gain survives against the same baseline given the same total compute, tuned as hard? A search that beats an untuned baseline has told you about your tuning effort, not about your architecture.

**eBay — a fraud GNN that had to forget the future and answer inside the request (2022)**

By 2022 eBay's risk stack already ran rule-based and machine-learning filters over every transaction. The case for a GNN was multihop risk propagation: fraud invisible in one transaction's own features but plain two hops away through a shared device, address or payment instrument. In a CIKM 2022 paper, eBay engineers with collaborators at ETH Zurich described what it took to put that in the request path; both obstacles were structural rather than statistical.

The first is temporal. A transaction graph is dynamic, and message passing over a static snapshot lets a target absorb information from transactions that had not happened when the decision was due. Their Two-Stage Directed graph splits the structure in two: a Batch Graph carrying bidirectional edges among historical reference transactions and the entities they share, and a Real-Time Graph whose edges run one way only, entity to target transaction. Nothing flows out of a target, so no message crosses between target transactions at different timestamps. The cost is real — a target contributes nothing to its neighbours' representations, giving up the mutual reinforcement that makes rings easy to spot offline.

The second is latency. A naive GNN at request time pays for the neighbour query and then multi-hop aggregation, which eBay measured in hundreds of milliseconds. The Lambda Neural Network splits the computation along the same seam: a Batch Net runs the deep convolutions over historical transactions and shared entities offline and flushes entity embeddings into a key-value store, and at request time an RT Net fetches those embeddings, takes the target's raw features, and runs a single convolutional layer.

On 7 million labelled transactions — a Two-Stage Directed graph of 66.4M nodes and 332.0M edges against 56.7M nodes and 153.9M edges in the static view — BRIGHT-LNN with a GCN backbone reached an average precision of 0.4420 ± 0.0035, reported as a 2.2% improvement over their LightGBM benchmark. End-to-end P99 latency fell from 251.35 ms to 72.57 ms on CUDA, a 71.13% saving, with model inference 7.87x faster. What was traded away is freshness: an entity's embedding is as old as the last batch, so a ring assembled between refreshes is seen only through the one live hop.

That trade is the decision this lesson prepares you for. Offline, deeper aggregation over a richer neighbourhood always looks better. In production you first draw the line between the hops you can precompute and the hop that has to be live, then check the direction of every edge against its timestamp — because a GNN scoring well on a static snapshot of a dynamic graph is often reading an answer it would not have had.

**Stanford Medicine — a 141M-parameter record model against counted codes (2023)**

EHRSHOT, released at NeurIPS 2023, is unusual for a clinical benchmark in that it ships the data and the pre-trained model together: 6,739 patients from Stanford Medicine, 41.6 million coded clinical events across 921,499 encounters, alongside CLMBR-T-base — a 141M-parameter transformer, twelve layers of 768 hidden units with a context of 5,952 clinical events, pre-trained self-supervised on the structured records of 2.57M patients. Fifteen downstream tasks in four families: operational outcomes, anticipating lab results, assignment of new diagnoses, and chest X-ray findings.

The opponent was deliberately dull. Count how many times each clinical code appears in a patient's history, put the counts into a gradient-boosted tree. No sequence, no representation learning, no pre-training — the tabular baseline any hospital analyst would write in an afternoon.

The headline is the one self-supervision promises. Aggregated across task categories, the pre-trained model beat the count-based GBM at every few-shot budget up to and including k = 64 labels per task. That is the claim worth having: representation learned without labels converts into performance exactly where labels are scarce, which in clinical work is nearly everywhere.

The result that earns the study its place is the reversal. On the assignment-of-new-diagnoses tasks, past k = 64 the count-based GBM overtook the foundation model. The authors attribute it to the pretext task — CLMBR is trained to predict the next code, while diagnosis assignment carries a one-year horizon, so the objective is a poor match; where a handful of codes correlate strongly with a diagnosis, a tree splitting on those counts directly beats a representation optimised to continue a sequence. A pre-training objective is a prior. Priors pay when data is thin and charge rent when it is not.

So the question to put to any self-supervised or foundation-model proposal on structured data is not whether it beats a tuned gradient-boosted tree, but at what label count, on your tasks. Fit the boring baseline with the same tuning budget, sweep k, and find the crossover. If your realistic annotation budget sits to the right of it, the pre-training has bought a serving dependency, a context limit and an inference bill in exchange for nothing you could not have had from counted features.

**Politecnico di Milano — eighteen neural recommenders, seven that ran, six that lost to nearest neighbours (2019)**

Maurizio Ferrari Dacrema and Paolo Cremonesi of Politecnico di Milano, with Dietmar Jannach, took eighteen top-n recommendation algorithms published between 2015 and 2018 at KDD, RecSys, SIGIR and TheWebConf and tried to stand them up again. The paper took the RecSys 2019 best long paper award, which tells you the community recognised the problem it named.

The first filter was reproducibility, defined generously: a working version of the source code available or needing only minimal modification, plus at least one dataset with provided or reconstructible train/test splits. Seven of the eighteen passed.

The second filter was a fair fight. Their baselines were unglamorous — TopPopular, ItemKNN, UserKNN, content-based and hybrid KNN variants, and the graph random-walk methods P3α and RP3β — but they were tuned properly, with Bayesian search over 35 configurations per algorithm-dataset pair, sweeping neighbourhood size from 5 to 800 alongside shrink terms and damping exponents. Six of the seven reproducible neural methods were beaten by that set. The seventh, Neural Collaborative Filtering, did clear the nearest-neighbour family — and then lost on MovieLens1M to SLIM, a linear model that predates the deep-learning recommender literature entirely.

The mechanism is not misconduct, which is why it survived peer review at four strong venues. It is asymmetric effort. Authors tune their own method exhaustively and inherit baseline numbers from earlier papers, where the baseline may itself have been untuned; every paper is locally honest and the aggregate is a trend line manufactured out of hyperparameter budget. The authors found the tell: code for the proposed algorithm was shared far more often than code for hyperparameter optimisation, evaluation, preprocessing and the baselines — precisely the parts that decide whether a comparison means anything.

Carry that into your reading. When a paper reports a delta, what decides whether to believe it is whether the baseline received the same search budget, whether the tuning and evaluation code was released rather than only the model, and whether the comparison was rerun by these authors or copied from elsewhere. If those answers are missing, the delta is unmeasured rather than small. And before adopting any published method, spend a day tuning the dullest baseline in its table — it is the cheapest experiment you will run, and in this literature it would have settled six of the seven live questions.
